content: 1. It is essential to ensure that patients understand and accept the care model and the setting in which palliative care services are provided. This includes clear communication about the goals and structure of the care being offered. 2. Continuous monitoring and evaluation of the palliative care service are necessary to determine whether the objectives of the program are being met effectively. 3. A hospital-based palliative care service requires a minimum staffing structure, including a doctor and nurses trained in palliative care and communication skills. As a baseline, training should include both theoretical components and at least 10 days of practical experience. 4. Doctors in palliative care should serve as team managers or members, with full-time or part-time availability depending on workload. They must have specialized training in palliative care and communication skills to address the needs of patients and their families. 5. Nurses, whether regular or visiting staff, are essential team members. They must also undergo training in palliative care and communication, with a minimum of 10 days of practical experience. Their availability can be full-time or part-time, depending on the service's needs. 6. Auxiliary nurses or palliative nursing aides assist staff nurses in clinical work. They may be regular or visiting staff and can work full-time or part-time. 7. Volunteers, while not mandatory, are recommended to provide additional support to the team. Their roles are specific to the needs of the service, and they typically work part-time on a visiting basis. 8. Palliative care for children encompasses physical, emotional, spiritual, and social care, addressing developmental needs from neonates to young adults. The family, including siblings and extended family, is considered the unit of care. 9. Pediatric palliative care is a specialized field that involves active, comprehensive care of the child’s body, mind, and spirit, while also supporting the family. It begins at the time of diagnosis and continues regardless of whether the child receives disease-directed treatment. 10. Health providers in pediatric palliative care are responsible for evaluating and alleviating the child’s physical, psychological, and social distress. 11. Approximately 2 million children require palliative care in the last year of their lives. The range of conditions necessitating palliative care in children is broader than in adults, including neonatal conditions, genetic anomalies, congenital conditions, neurological disorders (e.g., cerebral palsy), and rare diseases. 12. Pediatric palliative care can be delivered in various settings, including the home, primary health care clinics, hospitals, children’s homes or orphan care centers, day-care centers, pediatric services, general palliative care or hospice services, family medicine services, or hospice inpatient units. 13. In resource-limited settings, the minimum workforce for pediatric palliative care includes a nurse and a doctor with pediatric palliative care knowledge and competence, supported by community health care workers. 14. In resource-rich settings, the team may include a pediatrician, psychologists, social workers, and other allied health therapists. Nurses often serve as team leaders in many settings. 15. An ideal pediatric palliative care team includes doctors with pediatric expertise, registered nurses with pediatric experience, social workers, teachers, chaplains or spiritual care workers, and consultants such as neonatologists. All team members should have training in pediatric palliative care, communication skills, and an understanding of childhood development and children’s rights. 16. Essential requirements for a pediatric palliative care service include adequate staffing, access to essential pediatric palliative care medicines (preferably in pediatric formulations), materials for play and developmental stimulation, and age-appropriate nutrition. 17. The service must ensure children’s rights are protected, transport services are available, and there is a system for referring patients to other services, including transitioning to adult palliative care services. 18. Comprehensive record-keeping and the use of assessment tools tailored to different ages and developmental stages, including non-verbal children and those with neurological impairments, are critical. 19. Establishing a pediatric palliative care service involves conducting a needs assessment, reviewing child-related legislation, identifying required programs, forming a multidisciplinary team, running community awareness programs, and securing resources. 20. Policies and procedures, including fundraising and financial sustainability, must be developed. A referral system, ongoing training programs, and support systems for staff and volunteers should also be established. 21. A stand-alone palliative care center or hospice may serve multiple roles, including home-care services, inpatient care, day-care services, education, and research. The scope of services should be determined based on local needs, resources, and staff capabilities. 22. Hospice home-care services involve patients staying in their homes, with the hospice team providing medical care, nursing advice, and psychosocial support through home visits. A 24-hour telephone support service is essential, particularly in urban areas. 23. Inpatient hospice services provide care within the hospice facility, offering a controlled environment for individualized care. The level of care depends on staff capabilities and the hospice’s role within the healthcare system. 24. Hospice day-care services allow patients to remain at home while traveling to the hospice for medical consultations, nursing care, rehabilitation, and social activities. This model may include outpatient clinics and is resource-efficient for patients able to travel. 25. A palliative care center or hospice can also function as an education center, training its staff, other healthcare workers, medical and nursing students, and the public in palliative care philosophy and practices. 26. A research center within a palliative care facility fosters continuous improvement in care and contributes to evidence-based practices. All services should conduct audits and evaluations, but a research center emphasizes this focus. 27. Integration of care between hospital, hospice home care, inpatient hospice care, and day care is essential. Smooth transitions between services must be ensured to prevent any patient from being overlooked. 28. Before launching a palliative care center, it is crucial to plan publicity efforts, promote community involvement, and establish systems for referrals and information management. 29. The availability of essential medications, including oral morphine, and the assurance of long-term funding and suitable premises are critical considerations for a stand-alone palliative care center. 30. Staff must receive specialized training, and there should be provisions for continuing education. Community involvement and support are vital for the sustainability of the service.
